# The Goal Loop: Goal, Measurement, Effort

Hand a coding agent a slow test suite three times, with a goal, then a way to measure it, then a sense of how hard to try, and watch which of the three gets it to the finish line.

**[▶ Take this lab on the Zenable Learning Hub](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=goal-loop&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=goal-loop_readme)** — fully hosted sandbox environment, progress tracking, and a full-featured lab workspace.

Eligible paid Zenable customers get an OpenRouter key automatically in their sandbox. Take the hosted version of this lab, with the key already configured, at https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=goal-loop&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=goal-loop_readme.

**Duration** 75 minutes · **Difficulty** Intermediate

**Topics** `Software Development` · `Verification`

**Prerequisites**

- Completion of Foundations & Context Engineering, Part 2
- Comfort reading Python and a shell prompt

## Set up AI inference

Your sandbox has no hosted AI key. Automatic keys require an eligible paid plan and an available inference budget. Choose your own OpenRouter key, or use the local model and the lab's recorded-answer steps.

### Option A: use your own OpenRouter key

Create a key at [openrouter.ai/keys](https://openrouter.ai/keys). Then run this in the sandbox terminal, with your key in place of `sk-or-...`:

```bash
zenable-configure-inference sk-or-...
```

The command writes your key and the model settings into `~/.env` and configures every coding agent installed on the sandbox. Open a new terminal so your shell picks them up.

> [!WARNING]
> Your key goes in `~/.env`, never in the lab directory. Every attendee in the sandbox network can read the lab remote, and a key committed there is a key you've shared.

### Option B: use local Ollama (no key)

The sandbox runs [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) with a small model, `qwen3-nothink`, already downloaded and built. Point every agent at it:

```bash
zenable-configure-inference --ollama
```

Then open a new terminal. The model runs on the sandbox's CPU, so expect slower and weaker answers than a hosted model gives you. This option configures coding agents only. For steps that call Jev directly, follow the lab's recorded-answer instructions, such as adding `--fixtures` where shown. Those commands do not switch to recordings automatically.

<details>
<summary>Not on a Zenable sandbox?</summary>

For Option B, install Ollama from [ollama.com/download](https://ollama.com/download). `qwen3:1.7b` is a reasoning model, and thinking makes it very slow on a CPU, so the steps below build a copy with thinking turned off.

Download the model. Run this on its own and wait for it to finish, because the progress display takes over the terminal and swallows anything you paste behind it:

```bash
ollama pull qwen3:1.7b
```

Then build a copy of it with thinking pinned off. It reuses the weights already on disk, so there's no download and it finishes in about a second:

```bash
ollama show --modelfile qwen3:1.7b > Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|^FROM /.*|FROM qwen3:1.7b|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{- if and $.IsThinkSet (eq $i $lastUserIdx) }}|{{- if (eq $i $lastUserIdx) }}|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{- if $.Think -}}|{{- if false -}}|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{ if and $.IsThinkSet (not $.Think) -}}|{{ if true -}}|' Modelfile.nothink
grep -q '{{ if true -}}' Modelfile.nothink
ollama create qwen3-nothink -f Modelfile.nothink
```

Then set the variables below in your environment, for example in a `~/.env` file that your shell loads with `set -a; . ~/.env; set +a`. Claude Code reads the `ANTHROPIC_*` variables, and agents that speak the OpenAI API, such as Codex, read `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and `OPENAI_API_KEY`.

For Option A, with your OpenRouter key in place of `sk-or-...`:

```text
ZENABLE_SANDBOX_MODEL=anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api
ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=sk-or-...
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=
ANTHROPIC_MODEL=anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL=anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL=anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL=anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5
CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL=anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5
TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api
TYPESAFE_API_KEY=sk-or-...
```

For Option B:

## Getting started

_~10 min · Hands-on_

Let's get the repository and take a baseline reading before any agent touches it.

```bash
cd ~
git clone https://github.com/Zenable-io/labs.git ~/zenable-labs 2>/dev/null \
  || git -C ~/zenable-labs pull --ff-only
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/goal-loop
uv sync --locked
```

Have a look at what we're working with. It's a deliberately ordinary service: a SQLite database of orders and their items, a product catalogue, a price lookup against a small HTTP service, and JSON serialisation of the result.

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/goal-loop
find . -path ./.venv -prune -o -type f -name '*.py' -print | sort
```

```console
./src/ledger/__init__.py
./src/ledger/bench.py
```

The `Taskfile.yml` gives us three verbs, and we use all three:

```yaml
# Copyright (c) 2026 Zenable, Inc.
version: "3"

tasks:
  test:
    desc: Run the service's tests
    cmds:
      - uv run --locked pytest -q -m "not goal" tests

  bench:
    desc: Time the test suite and print the wall-clock seconds
    cmds:
      - uv run --locked python -m ledger.bench

  check:
    desc: Is the bench under the lab's target yet?
    cmds:
      - uv run --locked pytest -q -m goal tests
```

Now the baseline. The bench runs the whole suite, so it takes over a minute:

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/goal-loop
task bench
```

```console
task: [bench] uv run --locked python -m ledger.bench
bench: 63 tests passed in 91.3s
```

Sixty-three tests, and nearly a minute and a half. Write your number down; we compare against it after every round.

`task check` is the target itself. It runs the bench and asserts two things: every test still passes, and the time is under the limit. Run it now and watch it fail:

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/goal-loop
task check
```

```console
task: [check] uv run --locked pytest -q -m goal tests
F                                                                        [100%]
=================================== FAILURES ===================================
______________________ test_suite_passes_under_the_target ______________________

    @pytest.mark.goal
    def test_suite_passes_under_the_target() -> None:
        passed, elapsed = run()
        assert passed >= TESTS_EXPECTED, f"only {passed} tests passed; the suite must stay whole"
>       assert elapsed < TARGET_SECONDS, f"the suite took {elapsed:.1f}s; target is {TARGET_SECONDS}s"
E       AssertionError: the suite took 90.1s; target is 10.0s
E       assert 90.1076306249015 < 10.0

tests/test_bench.py:16: AssertionError
=========================== short test summary info ============================
FAILED tests/test_bench.py::test_suite_passes_under_the_target - AssertionErr...
1 failed, 63 deselected in 90.25s (0:01:30)
task: Failed to run task "check": exit status 1
```

The test is short enough to read in full. Note the second assertion: the suite has to stay whole. Deleting tests is the fastest way to make a suite faster, and the target refuses it.

```python
# Copyright (c) 2026 Zenable, Inc.
"""The lab's target: the whole suite, still passing, under the time limit."""

import pytest

from ledger.bench import run

TARGET_SECONDS = 10.0
TESTS_EXPECTED = 63


@pytest.mark.goal
@pytest.mark.integration
def test_suite_passes_under_the_target() -> None:
    passed, elapsed = run()
    assert passed >= TESTS_EXPECTED, f"only {passed} tests passed; the suite must stay whole"
    assert elapsed < TARGET_SECONDS, f"the suite took {elapsed:.1f}s; target is {TARGET_SECONDS}s"
```

Before each round we put the repository back exactly as it shipped, so every round starts from the same place:

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/goal-loop
git checkout -- . && git clean -fdq -e .venv
```

## Round 1: a goal, and nothing else

_~15 min · Hands-on_

First, the way most of us ask. One sentence, no number, no instructions about measuring.

### Claude Code
We use Claude Code's print mode (`-p`) so each round is one command you can re-run. `--permission-mode acceptEdits` lets it edit files without asking, and `--allowedTools` lets it run the project's tasks and `uv`. The prompt goes straight after `-p`, because `--allowedTools` takes a list and would swallow anything after it.

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/goal-loop
claude -p "The test suite in this project is slow. Make it faster." \
  --permission-mode acceptEdits --allowedTools "Bash(task:*)" "Bash(uv:*)"
```

If you'd rather watch it work, start `claude` in the project and type the same sentence into the chat instead. The same goes for every round below.
### VS Code
Open the repository as a folder: **File > Open Folder**, pick `zenable-labs/labs/goal-loop` under your home directory, and click **Yes, I trust the authors** if VS Code asks. Then open the Chat pane (Ctrl+Alt+I), pick Agent mode, and paste:

```text
The test suite in this project is slow. Make it faster.
```

The agent asks before running commands in the terminal. Select **Allow** for `task` and `uv`.

While it works, notice what it reaches for first. Most agents open the test files, find one obvious thing, change it, and report success in a paragraph that sounds finished.

When it stops, read the number:

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/goal-loop
task bench
```

Compare it with your baseline. It usually moves. It almost never gets anywhere near the target, and the agent rarely ran `task bench` at all; it changed code it believed was slow and stopped.

Have a look at what it touched:

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/goal-loop
git status --short
git diff --stat
```

**Question:** how did the agent decide it was finished? Open its summary and look for the evidence it gives. Is there a before and after number in it, or a sentence that describes an improvement without one?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Without a measurement in the prompt, the agent's only signal is its own reading of the code. It stops once it has made the change it believes in. The summary usually names that change and says the suite should now be faster, with no timing in it. Nothing in the prompt asked it to run `task bench` and check.

</details>

Reset for the next round:

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/goal-loop
git checkout -- . && git clean -fdq -e .venv
```

## Round 2: a goal and a measurement

_~15 min · Hands-on_

Now the goal gets a number, and the agent gets told how to read it.

### Claude Code
```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/goal-loop
claude -p "Make the test suite finish in under 10 seconds. Run task bench after every change and read the time it prints; that number is the only thing that counts. Do not delete, skip or weaken any test." \
  --permission-mode acceptEdits --allowedTools "Bash(task:*)" "Bash(uv:*)"
```
### VS Code
In the same chat, start a new session (the **+** button) so the first round's context doesn't carry over, and paste:

```text
Make the test suite finish in under 10 seconds. Run task bench after every change and read the time it prints; that number is the only thing that counts. Do not delete, skip or weaken any test.
```

This round takes longer, because the agent now runs the bench after each change, and the bench is the slow thing. That's fine. Watch the numbers it reports back to itself: each one is lower than the last, and each change is a different file.

When it stops:

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/goal-loop
task bench
git diff --stat
```

Most runs land somewhere between the baseline and the target. The agent fixed two, three or four of the six causes, saw a real improvement in the number, and stopped because the improvement looked like success. It ran the bench this time, but the prompt didn't tell it to keep going until the time was under the target.

**Question:** look at `git diff --stat`. How many files changed? The repository has six independent causes. Which ones did it find, and is there a pattern to the ones it missed?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The ones it finds first are the ones near the tests: the per-test database rebuild in `tests/conftest.py`, and the retry sleeps it can see in a traceback or a timing. The ones it misses sit in files an agent rarely opens when asked about a slow test suite: `pytest.ini`, `schema.sql`, and a settings class that looks cached but re-reads its file on every property access.

The missing index is in a `.sql` file, the retry policy is in a different module from the client that uses it, and the pytest plugin that throws away the imported package before every test is one line in a config file.

</details>

Reset again:

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/goal-loop
git checkout -- . && git clean -fdq -e .venv
```

## Round 3: goal, measurement and effort

_~15 min · Hands-on_

The last part is the one most prompts leave out: how hard to try, and what "done" means in a form the agent can check.

The repository's `task check` gives us that check. It exits 0 when the suite is whole and under the target, and 1 otherwise, so the prompt tells the agent to keep going until `task check` exits 0.

### Claude Code
This is what `/goal` is for. It keeps the agent iterating until the end state holds, with a small model checking each turn against it, so nobody has to type "keep going".

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/goal-loop
claude -p "/goal make the test suite faster until task check exits 0 without deleting, skipping or weakening any test. Run task bench after every change. Expect several rounds: there are several independent causes in different files, and each one you fix moves the number a little." \
  --permission-mode acceptEdits --allowedTools "Bash(task:*)" "Bash(uv:*)"
```
### VS Code
VS Code has no `/goal`, so the effort goes in the prompt itself. Start another new chat session and paste:

```text
Make the test suite faster until task check exits 0. Run task bench after every change and keep going until task check passes; do not stop at an improvement. Expect several rounds: there are several independent causes in different files, and each one you fix moves the number a little. Do not delete, skip or weaken any test.
```

If it stops and reports progress, reply with "task check still fails, keep going" and let it continue.

This is the round where the agent reads files it skipped before. When the obvious fixes stop moving the number enough, it goes looking for why, and that's when `pytest.ini` and `schema.sql` get opened.

When it stops, run the target yourself:

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/goal-loop
task check
git diff --stat
```

Success! If `task check` passes, the suite is under the target with every test still in it. If it doesn't, read the assertion message: it says whether the time or the test count was the problem, and the agent can take it from there.

**Question:** we gave the agent the same codebase three times. Which of the three parts made the difference, and why wasn't the measurement alone enough?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The measurement let the agent read the time after each change, and that's why round 2 got further than round 1. It didn't say when to stop, though. An agent that sees 88 seconds become 40 has evidence of success, and with no stated end state it treats that as done.

The effort part supplies the end state ("until task check exits 0") and a warning that one improvement isn't enough ("expect several rounds"). All three together are a loop the agent can run on its own: do something, read the number, compare it with the target, go again.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Where were the six?</summary>

One per file, and only all six together get under the target.

1. `tests/conftest.py`: the `connection` fixture drops and rebuilds the schema and re-seeds 800 orders before every test, committing once per order.
2. `src/ledger/config.py`: every `settings.<property>` opens `settings.yaml`, parses it and validates every section. The serialiser reads four settings per order.
3. `src/ledger/repository.py` and `schema.sql`: `list_orders` runs two queries per order, and `order_items` has no index on `order_id`, so each one scans the whole table.
4. `src/ledger/serializers.py`: the tree is walked once to dump it and again to validate it, and the validation is re-run on the whole order after every item is filled in.
5. `src/ledger/clients.py` and `src/ledger/retry.py`: a new client, with a fresh TLS context, is built for every price lookup, and the retry decorator sleeps and retries a 404, which is the service's normal answer for an item with no price.
6. `pytest.ini`: `-p tests.plugins.fresh_app` throws away the imported `ledger` package before every test, so the 40,000-entry catalogue is regenerated and re-indexed 63 times.

</details>
